subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of bill No. 149, to establish a Department of National Health and Welfare.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to establish a new department of government to be known as the Department of National Health and Welfare, under the direction of a Minister of National Health and Welfare. The bill carries out one of the undertakings in the speech from the throne which relate to the establishment of new departments of government to deal, amongst other things, with postwar planning. I shall read the passage from the speech:
My ministers believe that the time is rapidly approaching when a minister of the crown should be responsible for each of the three broad fields of post-war planning. You will accordingly be asked to approve the establishment of the following departments of government:
(1)	A Department of Veterans' Affairs to have charge of the rehabilitation and reestablishment of members of the armed forces, and the administration of veterans' pensions and allowances;
(2)	A Department of Reconstruction to promote and coordinate planning for national development and post-war employment; and
(3)	A Department of Social Welfare to organize and to assist in administering activities of the federal government in the fields of health and social insurance.
The words "Social Welfare" as the designation of the department have since been changed to " National Health and Welfare."
As to the scope of the new department, it divides itself broadly into two parts, the first of which has to do primarily with health, and the second with social welfare.
The first part, concerned primarily with health, takes over from the old Department of Pensions and National Health those branches which relate particularly to health. As the house is aware, there has already been taken from the Department of Pensions and National Health the .portion of the work of that department which relates more particularly to veterans' affairs. Apart from veterans' affairs, there remain the branches of the department which relate to national health. All these will be brought under the new Department of

Department oj National Health and W el! a re
National Health and Welfare, and the present Department of Pensions and National Health will disappear.
The other main division of the new department will be social welfare. This will include such branches of the public service of Canada as relate to social welfare which may be transferred from existing departments to the new Department of National Health and Welfare, as well as the administration of such new social welfare measures as may be enacted. As the house is aware, there are several social security measures which are already on the statutes and which are administered by different departments of government. One of these is that pertaining to old age pensions administration, which has been under the Department of Finance. The Minister of Finance has indicated that in some respects it would be preferable that a department other than the Department of Finance should administer the old age pensions. I cannot say just at what moment the transfer may be made, but, at some convenient time, the administrative work in connection with old age pensions will be transferred to the new Department of National Health and Welfare.
There is also the statute relating to pensions for the blind, the administration of which will likewise be transferred to the new Department of National Health and Welfare. At the last session of parliament a statute was enacted having to do with physical fitness. At the present time it is being administered by the Department of Pensions and National Health. It will now come under the new Department of National Health and Welfare.
A number of measures relating to social welfare and human well-being are contemplated in the programme of social security already outlined by the government. One of the most important of these is that which relates to family allowances. Hon. members will have seen on the order paper a notice which I have given of a resolution upon which a bill will subsequently be based dealing with family allowances. It is intended when that measure is enacted that it will be administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Hon. members will realize that the administration of a measure so important and far-reaching as that will require much careful preparation. It is therefore desirable that the new department should be formed at an early day so that the measure may be in full operation at the time fixed for it to come into force.
These were measures specifically set forth in the speech from the throne, but, in addi-

tion, the speech refers to some broader aspects of social security, and to these I should like to quote in the terms of the speech itself. One paragraph to which I would draw attention is the following:
A considerable measure of social security is already provided under federal and provincial legislation, but the working out of a comprehensive national scheme, in which federal and provincial activity will be integrated and which will include nation-wide health insurance, will require further consultation and close cooperation with the provinces.
It will be seen from this paragraph that the government hopes a means may be found of integrating matters relating to social welfare, to prevent overlapping and bringing about the effective coordination of activities as between the federal and provincial governments. We contemplate working out a comprehensive national scheme in which federal and provincial activities will be integrated and which will include national health insurance.
National health insurance is a subject which has already been referred to the important committee on social security which was appointed last session and again this session. This committee has been making a full and careful study of the whole question of health insurance. It will be necessary, at some stage, for the dominion and the provinces to have conferences in order to work out a comprehensive scheme which will serve the best interests of the dominion and provinces alike.
With regard to health insurance I would point out that it is a means to an end. The end of all this social legislation is social security. Social security will be brought about by such measures as will be undertaken under the veterans' affairs and reconstruction departments and those that relate to insurance against the social and economic hazards encountered in the life of the people. The necessity for a nation-wide plan must be apparent to everyone.
As was natural, the work of social welfare was taken up in the first instance by municipalities and the provinces. Many of the provinces have social legislation on their statute books to-day. They began first with such measures as those relating to workmen's compensation, mothers' allowances, child welfare, hospitalization and other social measures. More recently the provinces have been giving much closer attention to health measures. Some have departments or branches of departments dealing with health.
It has become quite clear that without some assistance and cooperation from the federal
JUNE 27, 1944	4261
Department oj National Health and Weljare
government there cannot be anything in the nature of a national scheme. Differences exist between provinces in connection with the legislation enacted. Nothing could be more inimical to a nation-wide plan than to leave to mere chance, and to conditions as they arise, the enactment from time to time by the dominion and by the provinces of different measures which may be regarded as necessary. There is a necessity for some central agency that can be helpful, in cooperation with the provinces, in coordinating services, in preventing duplication and overlapping, and in seeing, when one department is behind another in some important enactment, how that difficulty may be overcome. One of the functions of the new Department of National Health and Welfare will be to cooperate in that way with the several provinces.
There is no intention whatever in this enactment of attempting to invade the jurisdiction of the provinces in these matters. I will refer to that in just a second, but before doing so I should like to read another clause of the speech from the throne which relates to this matter. The speech contemplated that this nation-wide measure of health insurance would be effected only after there had been ample opportunity for study, in both provincial and dominion fields, and after there has been opportunity of conference between the provinces and the dominion. It is not the intention of the dominion to seek to force upon any province any legislation, no matter how good it may be, by invading provincial jurisdiction. What the dominion will endeavour to do in these matters is to bring about to the advantage of the provinces and the dominion alike, proper coordination of all efforts to improve the health and well-being of the people.
The speech continues:
When suitable agreements are reached with the provinces, my ministers will be prepared to recommend measures to provide for federal assistance in a nation-wide system of health insurance, and for a national scheme of contributory old age pensions on a more generous basis that that at present in operation.
That statement in the speech makes it clear that the dominion contemplates having at some time, we hope it may be soon, not only a nation-wide system of health insurance but, as well, a national scheme of contributory old age pensions. The administration of the contributory scheme of old age pensions would be a very important function of some department of government, and it is the intention to have the Department of National Health and Welfare administer the contributory scheme once it comes into being. In the interval one of the duties of the new department will be to help to gather the necessary
factual information which will be required in conferences between the provinces and the dominion, and also to gather from the experience of other nations the kind of knowledge which would be essential for the most efficient working of the old age pension scheme.
The Minister of Finance has made it clear that once the contributory scheme is enacted it will be possible for the government to consider, to use the words of the speech, a more generous basis than that which is at present in operation. "A more generous basis", I should say, would include a lowering of the age at which persons would become entitled to old age pensions and also an increase of the amounts of the pensions themselves.
Will the house pardon me if I mention that my colleague the Minister of Finance has just sent me a note indicating that this debate should be adjourned shortly in order to enable the bills respecting the amendment to the Bank Act and the Quebec Savings Bank Act to pass this house so that they can get over to the senate as soon as may be possible, because if they are to serve the purpose for which they are intended they will have to be assented to before the 1st of July. I will conclude more quickly than I otherwise would what I have to say on the second reading, and after a reply on the part of some hon. member opposite, with the permission of the house will ask that the debate be adjourned in order that we may take up the other measures.
I have indicated fairly well the scope of the work which the new department will be expected to carry on.. I should like, however, to set forth more concretely the different measures the department will be called upon to administer and over which it will have supervision. That cannot be better done than by quoting section 5 of the bill, respecting the duties, powers and functions of the minister:
5. The duties, powers and functions of the minister shall extend to and include all matters relating to the promotion or preservation of the health, social security and social welfare of the people of Canada over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, particularly the following matters:-
(a)	the administration of such acts of the parliament of Canada and of orders or regulations of the government of Canada as are not by law assigned to any other department of the government of Canada or any minister thereof relating in any way to the health, social security and welfare of the people of Canada;
(b)	investigation and research into public health and welfare;
(c)	the inspection and medical care of immigrants and seamen, and the administration of

speechtext:
What I have read, I submit, indicates a large number of matters with which the federal government is concerned in relation to health. So far as the municipalities are concerned, and on the question of any possibility of intervention there, the hon. member who raised the point would do well to read section 8 of the bill. I quote:
8. Nothing in this act or in any regulations made hereunder shall authorize the minister or
IMr. Mackenzie King.]
any officer of the department to exercise any jurisdiction or control over any provincial or municipal board of health or other health authority operating under the laws of any province. ,
The question of jurisdiction, therefore, need not be seriously raised ini relation to this measure.
As to the necessity for a measure of this kind, a great deal has been said, particularly since the beginning of the war, of the need to conserve human resources and to give them priority in our thoughts over the conservation of what are generally referred to as natural resources. There is no doubt that the views of the world are changing with respect to the weight to be given to human values in comparison with material wealth. Human wellbeing to-day has the place in the thoughts and minds of men and women of practically all countries which was given to material wealth in years gone by. In the early years of this country's history most legislation on so-called progress was concerned with the development of the country's resources, and that work will have to go on; it should go on. But too often in the development of our natural resources we have completely neglected, indeed we have in many cases destroyed, our human resources. There is no doubt at all that factory legislation and laws relating to social amelioration have been placed on the statutes for that very reason. It was recognized that without limitations as to the hours of work, without some regulation fixing minimum rates of wages and maximum working hours, instead of conserving our human resources we were helping to destroy them. In these last four years there has been so much in the way of destruction of human life that the world probably will not for generations to come be able to make up the loss of man-power, to say nothing of the undermining in many countries of the well-being of their peoples. For this reason the necessity for having a department of government which will deal with human welfare, which will be concerned primarily with human beings and their wellbeing, is becoming increasingly apparent.
In the past we have had, for example, our Departments of Public Works, and debates have been carried on at great length in this house in the discussion of public buildings, and other forms of public works. In comparison how much time has been given to discussions on those measures so necessary for the greater health and well-being of the population? Questions like this are forcing themselves to the front, and the time has come when it should be the obligation of some minister of the crown to be specially concerned
JUNE 27, 1944	4263
Department of National Health and W elfare
with matters that relate to human well-being and human welfare, whether they have been thought of in connection with provincial legislation in the past or whether both the provinces and the dominion have been concerned. Human personality, its recognition and development are of more importance than the protection of property, privilege or position and the increase of human well-being of infinitely more importance than the increase of material wealth.
The legislation which is before the house at the moment is for the purpose of developing a department of the federal government which will be primarily concerned with the human aspect of our national life. The new department will first of all continue existing services and functions of the national health divisions of pensions and national health. It will administer social security and welfare measures assigned to it from time to time. It will serve as a centre of planning and research in the fields of health, welfare and social security. It will coordinate federal administrative activities in the fields of health and welfare. It will assist in the coordination of health and welfare activities of the dominion and the provinces with a view to bringing about a comprehensive national scheme to include nation-wide health insurance; it will be charged with the administration of family allowances and when it is enacted with the administration of the national scheme of contributory old age pensions.
A word in conclusion as to one or two matters that the department will not immediately concern itself with. It is not a department' of social security. Social security is a comprehensive aim and is the objective of all social legislation. The means to that end differ. Health insurance is one of the means to that end. Health insurance and social insurance of other kinds are means of helping to ensure social security; but the most important means of achieving the end of social security is full employment. Therefore all measures that will contribute to full employment may be regarded as social security measures. But these must come under many departments of the government. For example, we have been discussing in the last few days, matters under the Department of Reconstruction which have to do with employment in one form or another. Employment is the concern of the Department of Labour and other departments of government. The Department of Veterans! Affairs is a department that by its different measures will help to effect social security. Unemployment insurance is one form of social insurance; it
100-268i
is not itself social security. It is a means, as I say, to that end. The administration of unemployment insurance is entrusted at the present time to the Department of Labour. At the moment it is not the intention to transfer its administration from the Department of Labour to the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the reason is obvious. A very important part of the work of the Department of Labour related to reconstruction is that connected with selective service and the various offices which have to do with employment services. These two-services are closely interrelated, for that reason alone it would not be desirable to think at present of transferring the administration of unemployment insurance to the new department. As time goes on, it may be, as social services increase, there will be here or elsewhere as between different departments of government of the federal administration, further transfers and arrangements.
The magnitude of the problems involved in a broad extension of social security and welfare makes it essential to have a separata department and a full-time minister, if the' federal programme is to be administered! efficiently and federal policies properly coordinated with provincial and local activities-..
We have talked a great deal about the new social order that is to come into existence after this war is over. Speaking on that subject, as I have from time to time, I have emphasized the note that unless that new social order is well under way before the war itself is over we may look for it in vain after that time. I hope that the measures which the government has introduced at this session, establishing these three departments, veterans" affairs, reconstruction, national health and: welfare, and1 all of which relate in an immediateway to post-war planning, are sufficient evidence that this administration has very much in mind the great social problems which will: confront this country immediately the war is; over, and that we are not waiting for the end of the war before providing the means needed properly to effect their solution.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. 149, to establish a Department of National Health and Welfare.

maintopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill affords me an opportunity to discuss what might be termed the almost forgotten man. Lest anyone should have any doubt as to the theme of my remarks this afternoon, I state now that I intend to deal with the Davidson cancer cure and try to give the latest developments which have taken place since this matter was first introduced into this house.
I was glad to note the reference by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the intention of cooperating with the provinces under this legislation. I know that that is extremely necessary, because under that musty old statute called the British North America Act, which was passed seventy-seven years ago, the federal government is pretty well tied up when it comes to dealing with matters within the jurisdiction of the provinces. That has happened in connection with the investigation which we tried to have into Doctor Davidson's work, and I think this bill will have the effect of creating a better understanding between the provinces and the federal government.
When I first undertook to press for a recognition of Doctor J. R. Davidson's work, I approached the medical association of the city of Winnipeg where Doctor Davidson resides.

I thought that that was the proper procedure to follow. However, I was informed that Doctor Davidson was a stubborn old man who would not play ball with the rest of the profession. That statement astounded me, because I was under the impression from my conversations with Doctor Davidson that he had offered everything he had discovered to the medical profession through the medical periodicals which are printed from time to time. However, he did tell me that there was some difference of opinion and that he found it better to explore his own clue and follow it through to the end without having any suggestions from others, however well-meAning they might be. He was carrying on his research work more or less independently of the medical profession. At all times the information in regard to his experiments was available to the medical profession if they so desired. I found Doctor J. R. Davidson of Winnipeg a very amiable and conscientious man, willing to cooperate with anyone, and as evidence of the truth of what I say I will read a short paragraph from a letter he wrote to the medical committee of the national research council when he applied for a grant. And by the way, let it be remembered that the medical committee of the research council refused Doctor Davidson the grant to carry on research work on the ground that the answers he had given to their questions were not on a scientific basis. Let me say in passing that I have never heard Doctor Davidson say one word derogatory to the medical profession or any person belonging thereto. This is what he writes:
It _ is my earnest hope that through the decision of your committee the medical profession of Canada will be able to preserve for the future whatever elements of value there may be in my treatment. In that event I would be happy and would feel that my life work had not been done in vain.
That is the attitude he took towards the medical profession even to the last, when he was turned down by the medical committee of the research council.
And now may I say a word with reference to the doctors. I know they can speak for themselves, but I have had a good deal of experience with doctors. They have helped me in many crises in my life, and I am not going to say that they are one of the finest classes of people; I will say that they are the finest men we have in our citizenry. More particularly do I say this having regard to the old pioneer doctors who, without the aid of automobiles or any of the other modern methods of transport, -went to their patients, no road being too long, no night too dark, no fee too small for those men in the pioneer
JUNE 27, 1944	4269
Department of National Health and Welfare
days. And all through the years the doctors have conformed to that pattern, even the modern doctors of to-day.
It has been said that I have no right to speak on a scientific question of this sort. Mr. Speaker, I speak from experience; I speak from the practical standpoint; and while I have said a word for the doctors, I am speaking at the same time for those who are afflicted with this terrible disease, and from my experience as a victim of it, coming from a clinic after an exploratory operation faking two hours. It was not just a physical exploration, because there is a ten-inch incision where they operated and found my case hopeless. I speak from experience, knowing what Doctor Davidson has done for me, and my heart bleeds for those in a similar condition. I therefore dare to get up and speak even on a scientific question.
I have done what I could to spread this gospel. Of 7,000 copies of the speech which I made in this house on February 7 last, over 6,000 have been distributed throughout Canada. I am receiving letters from all over the country, and public opinion is behind my efforts. If the government does not know it, it is time it did. I had occasion to be in Calgary during the first week of April and they arranged a meeting for me. We did not have a large meeting, but it was a meeting that was in deadly earnest, and I am still getting reports from people who are working throughout that city asking that the government take some steps to safeguard the discoveries of this great Canadian, Doctor J. R. Davidson. I had a meeting in my own city and later I am going to read a resolution that was passed there. I may say that a Mr. Pugsley, who represents the legislative committee of the railway associations of British Columbia, has been in Winnipeg during the past week making a private investigation of the work of Doctor Davidson. That is the work that is going on throughout the country, and yet we find the federal government and the government of Manitoba, who are just as guilty, passing the buck. There is no other term that fits the situation.
The resolution from which I am about to quote was endorsed by the city council of Portage la Prairie, by the rural council of Portage la Prairie, and, the other day, by the Manitoba federation of agriculture. I am not going to quote the whole resolution because it would take too much time.

maintopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext: Take time to quote it. It is important.

maintopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I want you to notice that the resolution asks for a full and fair investigation open to the press and to the public, and in passing I would say that the very opposite is the attitude taken by the medical committee of the research council. While I was in Winnipeg a representative of the research council said to me, "Mr. Leader, we will have an investigation if you are determined, but let it be in camera. These patients that you talk about do not want their private affairs exposed to the world. I think it would be better for you, for the patients, and for the medical profession, if we are to have an investigation, not to carry it out in the daylight." These resolutions, however, and the attitude of Doctor Davidson, request a fair investigation open to the press and to the public. Their idea is to let the people judge as well as the tribunal which will make the investigation. I quote from the report of the meeting that was held in Portage la Prairie:
A full and fair investigation into the Doctor Davidson cancer treatment, to be open to the public and the press, was also endorsed by resolution.
Reverting to the resolution passed at the meeting in Portage la Prairie, it was held under the auspices of the board of trade, being a mass meeting in the largest theatre in the city, which was filled almost to the doors. Those present were enthusiastic and the resolution was endorsed unanimously. I will not read the preamble, but here is the substance of the resolution-the Prime Minister has a copy; if he has not, then they did not follow my suggestion:
Now therefore be it resolved that in view of the ever growing menace of cancer ;to the national health, we urgently request the federal government and the provincial government of Manitoba, acting either separately or in cooperation, to hold without further delay a full and fair investigation into the Davidson cancer treatment. It is essential in our opinion that this investigation should be open to the press and the public.
Now perhaps a word in regard to mortality from cancer as compared with war. I made the statement last night to the Prime Minister that the matter which I wished to discuss was in my opinion, in some aspects, more important than even the war itself. Anyone who wishes to do so may qualify that statement, but in my opinion there are aspects of this disease which present a more important problem. In the first four months of the war-scarcely four months, in 1939-there were estimated to be 4,383 deaths from cancer.

4270	COMMONS

complete. In 1940 there were 13,332 deaths from cancer; in 1941 there were 13,417; and in 1942 there were 13,654. In 1943 there were 14,000; in the first six months of 1944-this is an estimate-there were 7,000. The house can see that there is a progressive increase year after year, and this goes on not only in war time but in peace time. One would think that any government or individual would be so keen to find anything that would stop the. ravages of this fatal disease that they would) jump at almost any clue that was submitted. That makes a total of 61,403 deaths. I have not the latest figures of the casualties of this war, but I think the number of heroes that we have lost amounts to 20,000. I think I am conservative in saying that that number have given their lives in the service of their country. That means that for every Canadian soldier who has lost his life so far in this war three people have died in this country from cancer. This would verify the statement that in some respects it is even of more importance from the point of view of casualties than the war itself.
Now, in regard to cancer, I am not a scientist, yet I have received information from those who are. I am told there is no cure for cancer unless it is treated in its early stages. That is the information I have received from the Mayo clinic; that is the information I have received from many doctors. Do not confuse my argument. I am not saying there is no cure for cancer, but I am saying on the authority of the best medical men in this country that there is no cure for cancer in its late stages. Doctor Davidson, that poineer doctor, when as a consulting physician in the hospital in Winnipeg he saw case after case of cancer coming in for treatment, diagnosed as cancer in which an operation was the only thing that would solve the problem or help the situation, and most of them dying, decided that he would give the rest of his life to trying to find a preventive. I want the house to remember that above all others his work has been along that line. He has been seeking the prevention of cancer rather than a cure.
Doctor Davidson believes that cancer is caused by a nutritional deficiency in our diet. I do not know how tru.e that is, but I can speak of my case. I would not be here to-day were it not for the vitamin treatment of Doctor Davidson in Winnipeg. You can take that for what it is worth. I have been told that the patients do not know anything about it. Well, we may not know how it is done, but we do know when it is done. Doctor Davidson is not the only man who has been experimenting along this line. I was told by a friend of mine in Winnipeg that I would find information in a publication, the name of which I

forget at the moment, but I think it is the annual review of the national research council, to the effect that many medical doctors are experimenting in England and in the United States, and quite a number in Canada and perhaps throughout the world along similar lines.

maintopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I know of three in
Ontario.
Mr. LEADER; They have been experimenting along this line, and some day we are going to honour the medical man who finds either a cure or a preventive for cancer. The medical profession is looking for it. Doctor Davidson said that he wanted the medical profession to receive all the information that he has. He believes that they are the ones who should carry on the work. With all these doctors and scientists throughout the world, along with Doctor Davidson, exploring the theory of deficiency in diet, it may be that he is the one who has the clue. Perhaps Doctor Davidson is the one who will show the light to the rest of the world in regard to the prevention of cancer. If we could get some preventive for cancer we would need no cure. That is obvious.
On this point I wish to say that I think more money-and I 'believe it was announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) last night-should be made available for research work, especially medical research, in Canada. But at the same time, if Doctor Davidson's work is ignored, how is it going to affect the young scientists who want to follow that line of work? It would not be an incentive to any young doctor to undertake this work if men like Doctor Davidson, a pioneer doctor, experimenting for over thirty years, and who has something which I will show the house before I finish if I am given the time, is ignored.
I said something about the medical profession not being keen on accepting Doctor Davidson's theories, and that is very evident. I wish to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that my last speech had much publicity. I had it printed in pamphlet form, and one of the requests I received came from one of the South American republics. I sent a number of copies and today those speeches are translated by the government into the Spanish language and are used by the government cancer clinic of the Dominican republic. I saw two letters in Doctor Davidson's office from research men- I believe they were institutes-asking Doctor Davidson if he would come to California and carry on his experiments there. I have recently received word that two requests have come from England for Doctor Davidson to give some information on his work and perhaps
JUNE 27, 1944	4271
Department of National Health and Welfare
emigrate to the old country. He does not want to go. Do we want to lose him? Is there not room in Canada for men of that type? I say to the Prime Minister that if Doctor Davidson's method is sufficiently attractive to foreign countries to cause them to seek information about it, it should be taken up by the Canadian government.
It is nearly a year since this matter came before the house. It was brought up by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and then by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden). Both hon. members suggested that the government should assist Doctor Davidson in some form or other to carry on his research work. As I said before, nearly a year has gone by. It might be well to go back and look at the figures I submitted a while ago. Approximately 14,000 of our people have perished from cancer in that time and no action has been taken. Speaking according to my own conscience, Mr. Speaker, I will say it would charge me with criminal negligence if I did not undertake to bring this matter before the house at every opportunity that presents itself until some action is taken by those in authority.
It would be unfair for me to leave the impression that the Minister of Pensions and National Health has not been very sympathetic; I believe he tried to do his best within his limited power, but sympathy is not going to get us anywhere in regard to this case. We want definite action.

It was first referred by the minister to the medical committee of the research council, which was not the proper thing to do, and I so stated in my first speech. Why? Because it was prejudged by some of the members of the research council, at any rate. That is not a proper tribunal to make an investigation into this matter. Nevertheless it was submitted to the national research council and they gave their verdict which, as I expected, was that Doctor Davidson was not entitled to a grant to help him carry on his work. Then the minister referred the matter to the Manitoba government, and asked the medical faculty of the university of Manitoba to conduct an investigation. The president of the university said they would be glad to do so, but made his acceptance provisional. He said, "We want to make a thorough investigation, and to call witnesses. This will entail some expense, which we expect the federal government to defray." That was the condition on which the university undertook to
100-269}
carry on the investigation. I know the minister explored the possibility of giving the province some financial aid, but came up against the British North America Act and could not make a move.
Then what happened? The minister referred the matter again to the national research council, and I do not agree with that action. Now let me give the latest information as to what the government has in hand at the present time. The document I have in my hand, which is authentic, declares that-
-the dominion has no jurisdiction to investigate its remedial aspects. It would, therefore, appear to be a provincial matter, and it is regretted that there is no further action which can be taken.
So it is left to the government of Manitoba, and! perhaps we should look into the attitude of that government, which is set out in a short quotation I have here. It is a statement in the press attributed to Premier Garson, and reads:
Premier Stuart S. Garson suggested in the-Manitoba legislature Monday that no financial assistance be given to Doctor J. R. Davidson of Winnipeg in his cancer research until a report on the work is made by the medical faculty of the university of Manitoba.
Mr. Garson said dominion pensions minister Ian Mackenzie had requested the medical faculty to conduct a further examination of Doctor Davidson's vitamin cancer treatment experiments. "We would be derelict in our responsibility if this house made a grant to assist Doctor Davidson before the report has been, received," he said.
To be fair to the premier of Manitoba it must be stated that when he made this statement he was under the impression that an investigation was to be undertaken by the university of Manitoba; but that is the attitude of the government of that province. Now I am coming to the most important part of my remarks.

The first letter is from the wife of a man who was suffering from cancer, and is as follows:
Dear Mr. Leader:
Received Dr. Davidson's letter to-day requesting we write you giving details of my husband's case. We have felt, like you, there should be some recognition of his treatment before his own health fails.
My husband's illness was caused by X-ray burns, the same being given for treatment of . cancerous growths. The first growth appeared on his forehead about eleven years ago and diagnosed as cancer. A skin grafting was done. Four years later another growth and more grafting. Two years ago another growth which did not respond to grafting and ulcerated. X-ray taken which showed bone involved and diagnosed carcinoma, type 4.
Dermatologists who saw him in Detroit in April, 1943, said he could live only a matter of a few months.
June 1943 doctors at Mayo clinic who saw X-rays said nothing more could be done.
In July he was losing weight and strength rapidly and weighed 149 pounds. Considerable pain in head. In desperation we left the 24th of. July for Winnipeg to see Doctor Davidson after reading in the papers about him. In fact, Mr. Leader, you opened Doctor Davidson's office door for us the morning we arrived. You were just leaving and Doctor Davidson told us who you were.
The first week in Winnipeg he spent in bed [DOT]except to walk from the Marlborough Hotel, one-half block from Doctor Davidson's office, *once a day. After the first week's treatment he was able to be up the greater part of the day. He now weighs 1C9 pounds-twenty .pounds gained and is very active with scarcely any pain. He continues faithfully with the treatment.
Doctor Davidson did not say he could cure him due to the extreme X-ray burn which destroyed cells of the skin but he did say he could retard the progress of the disease which he certainly has done and we are certainly grateful. My husband is only 44 years of age and he certainly is not willing to give up and
[DOT](Mr. Leader.]
has two lovely children to live for. If there is anything we can do please let us know. Thank you for the good work you are trying to do.
Sincerely,
(Sgd.) Mrs. Frank Penhole,
98 Gladstone Avenue,
St. Thomas, Ontario.
The next letter is from West Kildonan, Winnipeg, and is as follows:
Sir,
I am a housewife of Winnipeg.
I have had a very serious illness, and had to he operated on for cancer. The operation was performed on the 20th of March, 1943.
Afterwards my doctor said there was nothing more could be done for me and that I could only live six months, or a year, at most. I had heard of Doctor Davidson so consulted him. I underwent his treatment (and still do) and I must say that I have improved greatly from it. I have gained about seven pounds in weight. I eat well, and what is more important I sleep well, and I have every confidence in Doctor Davidson and feel quite sure I will be cured. I have been examined by my previous doctors (since undergoing this treatment) and they are astonished at the change and they report that there is no further growth of the cancer.
I had read of your taking up Doctor Davidson's case in the house so I thought I would write and let you know the benefit I have got from being treated by him.
Very truly yours,
(Sgd.) Mrs. Annie Faickney,
184 Belmont Avenue, West Kildonan, Winnipeg.
The next letter is from a gentleman who lives in Miami, Manitoba, as follows:
Dear Sir,
In 1939 I had a large painful growth on my left groin. I had it examined by five surgeons, including Doctor Rutherford MacCharles and they all agreed it was a sarcoma. The only treatment they could advise was an operation, and I was given to understand an operation for sarcoma was very unsatisfactory and usually caused it to spread to other parts of the body. I went, to Doctor Davidson and commenced the high vitamin diet and in November radio malt, wheat germ, high vitamin pills, etc. For two weeks I stayed in Winnipeg and he gave me a hypo in the arm daily of egg serum. I went home then and continued the diet and the fertile incubated egg treatment. The growth began to soften first and gradually got smaller. After a month's treatment I could walk short distances without pain. By spring the growth had disappeared and I had the full use of my leg again.
I went to Morden hospital near the end of March and had Doctor Menziers remove a gland where the growth had been and sent to Winnipeg for a biopsy but I was too late doing this as there was nothing left of it.
The treatment, in addition to taking away the growth, improved my health greatly. At fifty-seven I can do more heavy work on the farm than I could for many years.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) H. H. Storey.

Department oj National Health and Welfare

Beaver Valley Fur Farm,
Octsa Lake, B.C.
March 3, 1944.
Mr. Harry Leader, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
This letter is with reference to the treatment for cancer I received from Doctor J. R. Davidson of Winnipeg.
Here is a short history of my case. I went to Vancouver in January, 1942, where I was operated on and a growth removed from the womb. A frozen analysis was taken of the growth by the pathological at St. Paul's Hospital in that city and it showed that the growth was cancerous. The operation was followed by x-ray and radium treatments. When I got well enough I returned to my home and before six months were up found myself with a secondary growth in the bowels. I returned to Vancouver where they performed a colostimy operation, supposedly to relieve me. When I got back on my feet again after this operation they told me I would only live six months or a year at most which was quite a blow as I was only ' 32 years of age.
In March 1943 I went to Doctor Davidson and took his treatment for five months. At the end of that time I was so well I was able to come home. I have been home now for almost six months, feeling fine and able to do my own work.
Doctor Davidson's treatment benefited me to the extent that I know I would not be living to-day if it had not been for his treatment.
At the present time I am feeling fine and have no trouble except with the colostimy operation which was unnecessary in the first place.
My husband joins with me in wishing you every success in your appeal to the government for help for the doctor. We think he richly deserves it.
Yours very truly,
Mrs. Frances Eakin.

Dear Mr. Leader:
Having seen through the medium of the newspapers of the interest you are taking in trying to bring to the attention of the government the wonderful strides in cancer research being made by Doctor J. R. Davidson, of the Somerset Building Winnipeg, Manitoba. And feeling that every bit of evidence which may be placed in your hands should be provided, in order to get the government to realize that the Doctor is worthy of their support in every way. I am writing you this letter to be used in any way you think best, hoping that it may in its own poor way aid you in bringing about that recognition.
I was suffering from cancer of quite long standing and, like so many so afflicted, deferred getting medical attention until it was almost too late. Having the natural human antipathy to anything surgical, when I did commence to get medical advice about my trouble, tried those mediums which I believed would give me relief without recourse to the use of the knife. But to-no a vail, for these things did me no good whatever. Finally I heard from an acquaintance of long standing that she had been cured of a cancerous growth by taking the treatments-afforded by Doctor Davidson, and I became one of his patients.
Doctor Davidson did not mince matters when he examined me, but told me what disease I was suffering from and that it was a case of operation, for I had left it too long to be cured otherwise. _ But. I did start to take the treatments provided by him and continued -them for several weeks, as .a build up, preparatory to the operation. I am as convinced as I am that I am alive right now that the treatments that I received in Doctor Davidson's office- laid the; foundation for me to come through the operation as I have, for that is behind me now. I also-firmly believe that a continuation of the treatment for a period of time will eventually cleanse my blood of anything cancerous, and that I will' again be as healthy as ever I was in all my lifetime.
I believe that the citizenry of the country owe a great debt of gratitude to Doctor
4274	COMMONS
Department of National Health and Welfare
Davidson for his untiring research for a cure for cancer. I know that I do personally and I am sure that you are making no mistake in furthering his cause. I am.
Respectfully yours,

The next letter is as follows:
% Sobie Silk Shops,
Regina, Sask., Feb. 23, 1943. Mr. Harry Leader, M.P.,
Portage la Prairie, Man.
Dear Mr. Leader:
I have just received a letter from Doctor J. R. Davidson, Winnipeg, stating you have requested that patients who have been treated by him for cancer write to you direct, and it gives me a great satisfaction to be given the opportunity. Following is a brief history of my case and a statement of the present condition of my health.
I was operated on for an abdominal tumor *at the Grey Nuns hospital, Regina, on February 8, 1943. A large eyst envolving the right ovary was removed and section of same showed signs of malignancy. I was referred to the Cancer Clinic on report of section and was given a series of forty deep X-ray therapy treatments after which I was given a complete examination and informed there was not any sign of a recurrence. However, with the gradual return of pain even while I was still receiving X-ray treatments I naturally became alarmed. By the end of June there was a steady throbbing pain in my lower left side where an unnatural full-mess was evident. I attempted to go back to work in July (my occupation being that of a saleslady), but toward the end of the second *week in August I did not feel equal to work any longer. On the 16th of August I went to Winnipeg and consulted Doctor Davidson who immediately began treating me. At the end of five weeks of treatment the pain was definitely subsiding, and after ten weeks of treatment the pain was negligible and the distended feeling was also disappearing. By the time I had received three and one-half months' treatment I did not have any more pain, had more energy and slept better and felt better than I had for years. I came back to Regina on the 21st of November, have worked every day since and have gained in weight and strength while working.
Sincerely hoping Doctor Davidson's method of treatment of Cancer will be made available to all with the least possible delay, I am, Gratefully,
Perley B. Dohlen.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I do not in any way seek to curtail the remarks of the hon. member, and I quite agree that he should be given permission to continue until he has concluded. There are special reasons why I think the house should be specially considerate of the hon. member, when he brings forward a matter for consideration concerning which he feels as deeply as he does about the one on which he has been speaking. I believe, however, it is important that there should be some understanding as to the latitude to be allowed in the discussion of measures on second reading. We are now dealing with a bill to create a new department of government. It is a matter of administration, and the question for debate is as to whether a department is or is not to be established. We are not being asked to decide upon or to debate all the possible matters which may or should come before that department; we are not at present to discuss the merits or otherwise of such matters.
This afternoon the hon. member-and from his point of view, very sincerely-has been discussing the question of the treatment of cancer, and the action the government should take. It seems to me that is a subject which the house might properly consider when an
JUNE 27, 1944	1275
Department of National Health and Welfare
estimate is before us, as for example when we are discussing grants by the federal government to public bodies for purposes of research.
I do not see how we can possibly get through the business of the session this year if latitude of the kind being permitted at the moment to the hon. member is to be permitted in connection with the discussion of further measures.
I know that there was wide latitude granted in discussing the question of reconstruction, but matters of reconstruction were related immediately to the bill, because there is not in existence a department in the nature of a reconstruction department. But we have at the present time a Department of Pensions and National Health; it is in existence, and it seems to me that, if the particular subject of cancer research were to be discussed at all, it should be discussed in connection with the work of that department and not mixed up ' with the question as to whether we are to establish a new department of government. I submit very respectfully to Your Honour that there should be some very careful limitation placed on the rights of members when discussion takes place on all kinds of things on second reading of a measure that is specifically for one purpose and one purpose only.

Dear Sir:
I have been following your efforts as published in the local press regarding a government grant to Doctor J. R. Davidson to further his work on cancer research, and thought you might like to hear of my mother's case.
I took her to Dr. Davidson when she was eighty-one years of age. He has treated her for several years. Last summer she was able to travel to Toronto alone to visit Ed. Young, who is no doubt a friend of yours, as he was member for Weyburn for many years. She will be eighty-six in March. I would not say she has been cured, but the lump which had been diagnosed as cancer has disappeared from her breast and she has not suffered. It was difficult for the doctor to get her to eat the things she should as people of that age dislike changes in their diet. I
I am quite certain of one thiDg, and that is that she would not have been spared this long had it not been for Dr. Davidson's treatment.
I was in to see him a short time ago and he does not look any too well.
I do hope something will be done to further his work and honour him for he is a real doctor. If there is anything else I can do to help this worthy cause please advise me.
I might state that we are real old timers in \\ innipeg having lived here for over sixty years.
Yours sincerely,
A. W. Peebles.
814 2nd St. S., Kenora, Ontario, February 21/44.

Dear Sir:
I have been interested in your efforts to point out to the dominion government the valuable work being done by Dr. J. R. Davidson. As a recent patient, having been dismissed just three days ago with a 100 per cent cure, I would like to add my testimony in the hope that it may have some small weight in promoting Dr. Davidson's discovery.
A. short time ago I consulted Dr. Davidson with regard to a lump in my breast. I had known of this condition for over two years, but as it was not inconvenient or painful, I postponed medical attention. A few months ago the lump grew larger and I became worried. At the time I consulted Dr. Davidson I was very run down physically and suffering from nervous strain. When the doctor examined my condition he advised six weeks' treatments, diet, and injections, then an operation. After five weeks' treatments I. had an operation for breast amputation by Dr. Blakie. The quick recovery was marvellous owing to the previous build-up. Two days after the operation I was able to sit up for a short time and walk around the room without any feeling of weakness. Two days later I was allowed to leave the hospital. In one week from the operation I was able to walk to Dr Blakie's surgery, have the stitches taken out, then go over to Dr. Davidson's office and continue the injections. I took more injections for three weeks, then returned home. At the present time I am in better health than I have been for years.
I would like to think that something could be done to enlarge the field for this wonderful discovery. As things are now it is very difficult for people out of town to take advantage of the serum treatments. In my case it meant leaving my position and living away from home for weeks when the injections only take a few minutes a day. Then again, unless help is given only a limited amount of serum can be obtained' Having benefited so richly by these treatments myself and talked to many patients who, when hopeless, have been given a new lease on life, I would like to see these treatments within the reach of all who need them.
I sincerely hope that your efforts with the powers that be will be successful.
Yours sincerely,
Miss J. E. Waites.
Winnipeg, Man., February 21, 1914.
Mr. Harry Leader, M.P.,
Dear Sir:
I see by the Free Press that you are endeavouring to -further the research work of Doctor Davidson in his treatment of cancer. And I for ODe do want to add my own personal experience as to what Doctor Davidson has done for me. About two years ago I was very run down in health weighing only 137^ lbs. My normal weight before that was around 15o! in this iun down condition I developed a growth in my breast which caused me very much concern. I went to three or four different doctors in the city and they advised me to have an

Department of National Health and Welfare
operation and have it analyzed and if necessary have my breast removed. One doctor said I had a definite growth in my breast. Another doctor, one of the best authorities in Winnipeg on this sort of trouble, said there was no doubt it was malignant and strongly urged me to have an operation, which I very nearly did, but I am so thankful to-day that I did not. I was told about Doctor Davidson by a neighbour. I myself laughed at the idea of being treated by a diet. I mentioned this to a couple of the other doctors, giving no names; one said, don't be foolish. The other said, you are just loosing good time. My health being so run down I was really afraid to chance the operation so I thought I would go and see Dr. Davidson anyway and see what he had to offer me. The very first thing he told me was that I was very run down and removing the breast would not cure the trouble. So he made out a complete diet of very nourishing foods, also advised me to take plenty of wheat germ, raw milk, etc., and gave me a prescription of vitamins to take. I began to regain health and strength almost immediately. It took quite a few months for the growth in my breast to disappear, but as I got stronger and my normal health and weight returned, this trouble has entirely disappeared, taking the growth with it. I would be more than willing now to have any doctor examine my breast and I certainly give Dr. Davidson all the credit. He saved me from an operation and most likely death, for I was in such a run down condition; none of the other doctors that had advised me to have an operation ever considered my run down condition. This is one point I especially do credit Dr. Davidson with. Now my general health is fine, I can now do all my own house work and just about back to my normal weight which I never thought I would be. Everyone saw me failing and wondered what was wrong. I only hope that more of the doctors would get next to this sort of treatment *by building up the body to resist growths, which I have proven to be a fact, much superior to the knife.
Yours very sincerely,
Mrs. Ben Hardy,
56 Ruby Street.
I just want to conclude by asking this question: Is the Davidson treatment effective? If it is not, the public is being duped. In either case a thorough investigation should be instituted. All we want is a fair investigation to allay the suspicion which has been aroused in the public mind and to get to the bottom of this thing. I am sure that no one, certainly not myself, and I do not believe Doctor Davidson, would for a moment question a verdict brought in by a competent tribunal. If Doctor Davidson has got something, the world should know it. If he has not, the public should know that at once.
I conclude by saying that now that health is to be considered a provincial matter the federal government should make a grant to the province of Manitoba or to the university of Manitoba in order that this investigation may be made. We want the investigation
to be made at the very earliest opportunity, and we want it to be free and open to both the press and the public.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the substance of my whole remarks, that a proper investigation be made of Doctor Davidson's work; and that can be done only by furnishing the necessary funds from the federal treasury to the province to make the investigation. I thank the house for its courtesy.
Mrs. CORA T. CASSELMAN (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my very great pleasure at the setting up of this Department of National Health and Welfare.
Health is under provincial control chiefly, and we already have progressive legislation and effective administration in many of the provinces. But there are many inequalities between province and province, complicated at times by the question of domicile. That is particularly so when the province passes the responsibility on to the municipality. The federal department has given increasing assistance in recent years, especially through its research bureaux and publications and through consultation with provincial administrators. All these contribute to the welfare of the people. But there is a much wider field, that of curative and preventive medicine, which affects the individual more directly. Two provinces have tried to bring in broad health acts, Alberta in 1935 and British Columbia in 1936, but they found too many complications for provincial control alone.
In the parliamentary social security committee, of which I am a member, consideration is being given to a dominion health bill. Study has been given to this matter by men who have wide knowledge concerning the legislation of other countries. It is remarkable that the three countries with the highest standard of living have been slow in producing an over-all health bill-Canada; and Australia is just now considering a further extension of its health measures. Progress in the United States has been slowed down to some extent. This may be owing to the fact that these are federal states and that these other countries, like ourselves, have difficulty in arranging matters which are partly under one jurisdiction and partly under another. I hope that consultation on these matters between the provinces and the dominion will straighten out these matters in order that the new department will have the power to go ahead with the plans placed before it.
I hope that we shall have the health bill before the house during this session and I will reserve any discussion of its terms until that time. If such a measure is adopted it
4278	COMMONS
Department of National Health and W elf are
will go a long way toward raising the whole standard of living in this country. Sir William Beveridge has stated that one of the two main causes of poverty is illness with its attendant loss of income, and large doctors' and hospital bills. Many a family dates its fall from security to an expensive operation or the long-continued sickness of one of its members. The adoption of health insurance would prevent these heavy expenses from falling all at one time. Year by year payment of premiums will spread the cost of treatment. There will be a spread among those who have different incomes as well as a spread over the years for the individual. Preventive measures will reduce the incidence of disease. Then, too, all income will increase in value. There will be more left as purchasing power for other needs, because medical and hospital charges will be borne by the insurance fund. Old age pensioners will benefit, as will all children under sixteen years of age, and many others whose medical bills will be paid through health insurance. Think of the peace of mind in knowing that there is benefit by health insurance right through all the years of one's life. Through the cooperation of the provinces and the dominion there should be a much healthier population. The national fitness bill which was passed last year is just now coming into operation and will play its part in building up the positive health of the nation.
The second responsibility of this new department of welfare was also allocated to the provinces by the British North America Act. Each has set up its own machinery and most provinces provide for mothers' allowances, widows' and orphans' benefits and workmen's compensation. The federal and provincial authorities share the administration of old age pensions, while unemployment insurance is under the dominion. Canada has recognized already the need, and partly applied the remedy, but it is not broad enough, not deep enough; there are too many gaps and inequalities as between province and province. This dominion department should help to eliminate some of these inequalities.
I am most anxious to see the benefits to. be provided by this social welfare measure set at as high a level as possible. We want to make available a decent standard of living. We want to see that the basic needs of food, housing, clothing, cultural privileges and recreation are provided. This income security should be a stabilizing influence in setting a level below which no one's income may fall. It is recognized in all these studies that there must be measures to ensure full employment. That is

fundamental in providing a satisfactory standard of living in any country. Our aim is full employment of man-power and resources, but there will be emergencies when the individual finds it impossible to provide for himself through his own exertions. Then the state must come to his help.
This question of social welfare was one of the subjects of deliberation at the recent Philadelphia conference of the International Labour Office which I had the privilege of attending. I was assigned to the committee dealing with social insurance and medical care. The Canadian government delegation was in general agreement with practically all the recommendations made in the comprehensive survey. These run to many pages and seek to make continuous a minimum level of income regardless of the interruptions caused by those five great evils which Sir William Beveridge calls want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. I should like to quote from the official bulletin of the International Labour Office. First I quote from paragraph 2 on page 6, which reads:
Income security should be organized as far as possible on the basis of compulsory social insurance, whereby insured persons fulfilling prescribed qualifying conditions are entitled, in consideration of the contributions they have paid to an insurance institution, to benefits payable at rates, and in contingencies, defined by law.
I wanted to read that because of the word "compulsory" which was put in at the suggestion of the workers' delegation. Next I read section 7 on page 7, as follows:
In order that the benefits provided by social insurance may be closely adapted to the variety of needs, the contingencies covered should be classified as follows:
(a)	sickness;
(b)	maternity;
(c)	invalidity;
(d)	old age;
(e)	death of breadwinner;
(f)	unemployment;
(g)	emergency expenses; and
(h)	employment injuries.
Provided that benefits should not be payable at the same time for more than one of the following contingencies: invalidity, old age and unemployment.
I read that to show the broad coverage which was discussed similar to that found in the Marsh and Beveridge reports. The suggestion was made that all these measures could not be put into effect at one time because of lack of trained personnel to carry them out. We will remember that there was some difficulty when we brought in unemployment insurance because of lack of trained
JUNE 27, 1944	4279
Department oj National Health and Welfare
personnel, a very important item in putting into force any measures such as these. I quote now from paragraph 22 on page 8:
Benefits should replace lost earnings, with due regard to family responsibilities, up to as high a level as is practicable without impairing the will to resume work where resumption is a possibility, and without levying charges on the productive groups so heavy that output and employment are checked.
I read that to show that the International Labour Office and others who have drawn up somewhat similar plans realize that there is a danger that income security may be coupled with indolence, complacency and unpreparedness on the part of the individual. That contingency has been considered and met by the provision that the thrifty and provident may increase their earnings through their own efforts and that those who do so will have a higher income. There is a fear in some quarters that those who show good common sense and prudent management in their economy will have to pay for the shiftless who will not take advantage of their opportunities. Mr. Churchill referred to this in one of his speeches. In order to prevent this, contributions are required from individuals during their earning years.
In New Zealand a registration fee, as well as income tax, is required. I asked Mr. Walter Nash how they collected the registration fee, and he said the applicant had to show his registration card when asking for employment. That would look as though the right to work is conditioned by the payment of the basic fee. You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that I tried to inform the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) of that fee on June 2. I should like to quote from an official publication entitled "Social Security, Monetary Benefits and War Pensions in New Zealand", as follows:
For the purpose of providing the necessary finance the act-
That is the social security act of 1938.
-establishes in the public account a separate account, called the social security fund.
Every person of the age of sixteen years and over is required to register under the act and, unless exempt, pay a registration fee, which for youths aged sixteen to twenty years and all females over sixteen years of age is 5s. a year, and for all males over twenty years of age 5s. a quarter.
In addition to the registration fee there is payable into the fund a social security contribution calculated at the rate of Is. in the pound on all salaries, wages, and other income, and any other moneys that may be appropriated by parliament for the purposes of the social security fund, or that may otherwise be lawfully payable into the fund.
It will be noted that the rate is one shilling in the pound for every pound of salary. There is no graduated scale of income tax for this fund in New Zealand. The poor man pays as much proportionately as the rich man. In the case of our income tax a much higher rate is taken from the rich. The chief virtue of New Zealand's measures is, I think, the completeness with which they cover the contingencies that may arise. We admire the manysidedness of the programme in New Zealand and Australia, and in that connection I would read a couple of paragraphs from a speech delivered at an International Labour Office conference by Mr. Barnard, chairman of the Australian parliamentary social security committee; and a member of the house of representatives:	.
In 1943 widows' pensions, invalid pensioners' wives' benefits, old age pensioners' funeral benefits, and a new style of maternity benefits were introduced with the support of the committee. More recently, unemployment and sickness benefits, and pharmaceutical benefits were passed into law. These two pieces of legislation will not begin until the government departments concerned have been staffed to operate. This should involve a delay of only a few months. The Australian government is meeting the cost of providing the people with these services out of the nation's consolidated revenue, and also from a special welfare fund established in 1943. The fund is financed by a graduated tax on all incomes and is collected through ordinary revenue channels. $90,500,000, or 25 per cent of the annual total amount collected in direct taxation each year, is paid into the fund.
I think it is worthy of note also that most of these benefits are at a minimum level in New Zealand and Australia. The New Zealand pound is worth around $3.50 of our money. The old age pension stands at thirty-two shillings a week for an unmarried person, and that works out at $25 a month in our Canadian funds. New Zealand, however, is ahead of us in making more liberal allowances for retention of property and1 other income. Their social security act of 1938 provides for universal superannuation benefits and states definitely that no person may receive these two benefits at the same time. Of course, to qualify for universal superannuation the individual must pay his contributions from time to time to the social security fund. The Australian benefits are not high either. Children's allowances begin with the second child, and are five shillings a week.
One more sentence from Mr. Barnard's address:
While these are not regarded as being by any means a high standard of subsistence, they form a basis upon which our social legislation can be built in future years.
I simply want to give these facts to the house, because I believe that a knowledge of
4280	COMMONS
Department oj National Health and Welfare
the underlying principles which have guided our sister dominions along this line should enable us to create a stronger department and to pass better measures for the department to administer.
There is much that I should like to say on this topic, but I will refrain from saying anything more at the moment. As we move forward along these lines we are inspired by the high ideal of bringing the ordinary comforts to all our people. Of course, that in itself will not bring them happiness, because I believe that your chief happiness consists in what you are and not in what you possess. It consists in being and not in having. And yet, as we enter this new age, which I firmly hope will be one of greater prosperity for everyone, and which will lessen man's inhumanity to man, participation in organizations such as the International Labour Office and other conferences in which Canada is represented can be of great help to us in instituting these services and in coordinating all our efforts in this direction. To gain and enlarge freedom from fear and from want is our objective.
